title: Daily Debrief — Tuesday, Nov 17, 2026: Nvidia's quarter, line by line

Daily Debrief · Tuesday, November 17, 2026

Nvidia's quarter, line by line

with tonight's changes; this replaces the earlier debrief.

Nvidia beat on almost every line and guided above the Street, and the market spent the evening deciding that was already priced. SPY fell 1.0% to $732.44, wicked under its 200-day and closed back over it. Nvidia is the centerpiece tonight, then the best trades for Wednesday from a scan of all 34 names.

The one thing

NVDA's after-hours pop (+4.8% to $162.90) faded to +1.0% overnight, and $170 is the line: your 0.786 ($170.22), the Nov 13 high and the straddle's upper breakeven all sit there. Under it, this is a bounce in a downtrend, not a turn.

For SPY the line is the 200-day ($729.79). It held on the close by $2.65 after a wick to $727.00, and the double top's measured target ($725.08) is just under it. A close under $725 and the market is in a new phase; until then we trade names, not the index.

Owning the misses: the PLTR $180 call closed −$486 intraday. That was the "uptrend + RSI<40" idea, and it should have been cut on Nov 16 when your 1.382 broke. The DAL $90 call is now −$432 on paper, bought after the move was done. And the V $440 call idea died before it started: V closed $416.77, under its $423 stop.

The trend behind our trades

Yields eased a touch (10-year 5.10%, 2-year 4.80%) while the dollar sits near its highest since April 2025 and gold is down 7% in a month. A firm dollar and falling gold with yields near 5% is the market saying real rates stay high: the Fed is expected to hike, not cut. That's the headwind for anything priced on far-off earnings: PLTR, NOW, SHOP, HOOD.

Oil is off 13% in a month despite renewed US–Iran fighting around Hormuz, because the IEA sees a surplus. That keeps the airlines (DAL) and cruises (RCL, CCL) fed, and takes the bid out of XOM. The fear gauge (VIXY) is up 23.5% in a month and the VIX rose four days in a row: fear is rising into a market that is only 6% off its high.

The centerpiece

Nvidia Q3 FY27, line by line

The short version

  • Demand: stronger than anyone modeled. Revenue $115.8B against a $108B guide; Rubin did close to $20B in its first production quarter; the cloud backlog was put at "$2.5 trillion".
  • Guidance: raised. Q4 revenue $130.0B ±3% vs about $125.25B expected; gross margin 71–72% (the bottom they already flagged); fiscal 2028 growth view up to about 75% from about 70%.
  • Biggest worry: Nvidia is now financing its own buildout. Guarantees rose to $118.0B (from $108.5B), supply commitments to $390B, total future commitments $518B, and receivables stretched to 64 days.
  • Chart: leans down, with one live bounce. Your 0.5 ($155.33) held on the 2-day close again; the 2-day still has eight lower highs in a row. The line that decides it is $170: your 0.786 ($170.22), the Nov 13 high and the straddle's upper breakeven all sit there.

1. The scoreboard

Every line beat except one: the AI clouds and enterprise bucket ($47.5B vs $48.4B), the newer, more financed customers. The hyperscalers did the heavy lifting.

Revenue $115.8B vs $109.15B Street vs $108B guide · Data center $107.6B vs $101.85B · Hyperscale $60.1B vs $54.1B · AI clouds/enterprise $47.5B vs $48.4B (miss) · Edge $8.2B vs $7.49B · Q4 guide $130.0B vs $125.25B

What matters most: revenue landed $5.6B above the top of their own range, and margin came in at the top of its range while Rubin ramped. A beat that big with no margin give-back says pricing held. The one miss, in the newer AI clouds, is the customers Nvidia is helping to finance.

Housekeeping: Nvidia no longer breaks out gaming, pro visualization or automotive. It now reports Data Center (Hyperscale; AI Clouds, Industrial & Enterprise) and Edge Computing ($8.2B). The old graphics segment was $9.8B, up 25% on the quarter.

2. The guide is the stock

The quarter tells you what happened. The guide tells you what you're paying for. Q4 at $130.0B is $4.75B (3.8%) above the published Street number. But the published number wasn't the bar. Solus's Dan Greenhouse said the buy side wanted "guidance of $130 billion", and UBS expected about the same. So the guide met the whisper, it didn't beat it. Q4 also has a 14th week, so part of that $130B is an extra week of sales.

History says that matters. The four reports from Aug 2025 to May 2026 were all beats, and the stock fell the next day every time (−0.4% to −5.5%). The one that broke the pattern, Aug 26, guided $108B against $103.9B, a 4% clear of the whisper, and rose about 7–9% the next day. Tonight looks more like the first group: the stock was +4.8% at the 8 pm after-hours close ($162.90) and +1.0% ($156.94) on the overnight venue near 11 pm. Nvidia beat by $7 billion, and by midnight the market had given back four-fifths of the pop.

The margin guide (71–72%) is exactly the bottom they flagged in August, with 72–73% for fiscal 2028. No surprise there, good or bad. The raise to about 75% growth for fiscal 2028 is the real new information, and Goldman leaned on it tonight.

3. What management said about the road ahead

  • Who spoke: Colette Kress, now interim CEO and still CFO, ran the call; chair Harvey Jones opened on the leadership change.
  • Rubin: "off to an explosive start", about $20B in its first production quarter, which they called the fastest ramp in their history. Vera Rubin Ultra is "on track" for next year, Feynman for 2028. Blackwell Ultra got credit for the year-on-year margin gain; the quarter-on-quarter dip is the early Rubin ramp.
  • Demand visibility: the cloud backlog is "$2.5 trillion", up from $2 trillion three months ago. Kress: demand is "continuing to outpace supply". B300 rental rates are up more than 60%, so the older chips are not being dumped.
  • Supply limits: wafers, substrates and advanced packaging, with new supplier deals (Amkor, Samsung Electro-Mechanics, SPIL). Kress did not name HBM memory or CoWoS on the call, but the $390B of supply commitments are mostly multi-year memory buying, so memory is where the money is going.
  • Power: "land, power, and shell" is "such a critical part". Customer sites running late is now a named risk.
  • Sovereign and enterprise: sovereign AI revenue more than tripled from a year ago; enterprise is expected to more than double in fiscal 2028, led by financial services. Australia: up to 2GW of capacity by 2027.
  • China: Q3 included $2.4B of licensed Hopper sales; "we are no longer shipping" them, and Q4 assumes zero China data center compute. New Commerce rules landed this week; the board formed an export-control oversight committee.
  • Financing: guarantees are $118.0B, including $105.0B of credit support for SB Energy campuses leased to OpenAI for up to 20 years. No payments made so far. Kress: they will be "disciplined and selective" and will "remain thoughtful in how we participate". Priority order for cash: supplier prepayments, then selective customer support, then buybacks.
  • Money plans: $28.1B returned in the quarter (a record), $150B added to the buyback ($227.3B left, to be used by end of fiscal 2028), dividend $0.25. Nvidia also agreed to buy Hugging Face.

4. What they worry about, and what they dodged

  • 1. Site readiness and power. Customer data centers that are "delayed or they have a challenge in terms of building that". This is the first time it's a named drag, and the post-election state moratoriums make it worse.
  • 2. Supply cost. "a significant change in terms of the cost of supply". That's memory. It's why Q4 margin steps down to 71–72% even as revenue jumps $14B.
  • 3. The balance sheet doing the selling. $118.0B of guarantees, $32B of neocloud commitments, $20B of equity commitments to labs and financiers, inventory up to $39.7B from $31.6B, and receivables at 64 days (60 last quarter). A $1.8B impairment on private holdings shows some of those bets are already marked down.
  • 4. Export rules and China. Zero is in the guide, so it can only surprise up, but the new rules are unpriced.
  • 5. Leadership and the investigation, which the release now lists as a forward-looking risk.

What they dodged. The board said up front it would not take questions on Huang's exit, and his name was never said on the call. UBS asked about long-term pricing against custom chips: "something for the future". Cantor asked how far vendor financing can go: no limit given. Goldman asked for hurdle rates on that financing: none given. Morgan Stanley asked whether the "100% demand" framing still holds: not answered directly. Nobody addressed the roughly $500B chip-financing platform that was reported to be in the works with Goldman. The things they wouldn't size are exactly the things a bear would want sized.

The big worry: the debt-funded buildout, both ways

What would ease it: the guarantees never get called (none have been so far); hyperscalers, who pay their own way, keep growing faster than the financed clouds (they did this quarter, $60.1B vs $47.5B); the Fed stops hiking, which lowers the cost of every lease Nvidia is backing; receivables come back toward 60 days.

What would make it worse: the Fed hikes on Dec 9 (markets price 91–97%) and keeps going, as St. Louis Fed president Musalem suggested tonight; a large AI lab misses a lease payment; states slow data-center permits, so sites sit idle while leases run; memory prices keep rising faster than Nvidia can pass them on.

How Nvidia is placed: $43.8B of free cash flow in one quarter and $53.5B of cash cover a lot. Total guarantees are about 2.7 quarters of free cash flow. The risk isn't solvency; it's that a slice of reported demand is demand Nvidia helped pay for. If you want one number to track each quarter, track that $118.0B.

5. The CEO question

  • Who ran it: Kress, in both jobs. No separate CFO was named. Chair Harvey Jones read the leadership statement.
  • Huang: Jones said he "voluntarily resigned" and that "the board has no intention of bringing him back". He is off the board, with no advisory role mentioned. Huang has said publicly he would "be honored" to return. He testifies before Congress on Dec 1.
  • The search: Heidrick & Struggles, internal and external candidates, no timeline. Jones: "we don't want to hurry".
  • The investigation: an independent board committee is still working; CNBC reported it covers sales to Megaspeed. Reports say the SEC is looking at the departure too.
  • How it sounded: controlled and dull, which is the point. Morningstar's Brian Colello: "Seems like business as usual". Kress closed with "We've got this." Reuters' read, which I share: demand is not the near-term risk any more; execution and governance are.
  • How much rests on one person now: more than before. Kress is carrying the CEO and CFO jobs through a Rubin ramp, a congressional hearing and an open investigation. Until a permanent CEO is named, every rally carries a governance discount.

7. The read-through

Everyone tied to the build rallied after hours. Then most of it faded overnight with Nvidia.

At the 8 pm close: DELL +6.2% · BE +7.2% · DRAM +5.5% · SMCI +5.3% · MU +4.7% · TSM +4.6% · NVDA +4.8% · ORCL +4.0% · AMD +4.0% · SMH +3.9% · AVGO +3.0% · INTC +2.7% · GOOGL +1.2% · AMZN +0.9% · MSFT +0.9% · META +0.7%

  • Winners: memory (MU, DRAM). $390B of supply commitments, "mainly multi-year memory procurement", is a purchase order for them, and the margin guide says Nvidia is paying up. Power (BE): "land, power, and shell" is the named bottleneck, and Bloom sells the power. Server builders (DELL, SMCI) ride the Rubin rack volume, though DELL reports Nov 24 and SMCI has thin margins. TSM makes the chips and the new packaging deals.
  • Mixed: AMD and AVGO. A bigger pie helps, but Nvidia's 75% growth view says it is not losing share. ORCL bounced 4%: OCI is a named Rubin customer, but Oracle is also the most debt-funded builder on our list, and its earnings (Dec 14) will be about financing.
  • Losers, quietly: INTC. Nvidia's 13F shows it cut its Intel stake by 25% (about $5.5B) in the quarter. INTC still rose 2.7% with the group, which tells you the after-hours move was a sector bid, not a view on Intel.
  • The buyers (MSFT, AMZN, GOOGL, META): under 1% each. Their capex is Nvidia's revenue; a bigger Nvidia guide means bigger bills for them. The market isn't rewarding the spenders.

8. The IV crush lesson, with real numbers

IV (implied volatility) is the price of uncertainty inside an option. Before a report it's high because nobody knows the number. The moment the number is out, that uncertainty is gone and the option loses value even if the stock moves your way. That's IV crush.

The straddle buyer was right that NVDA would move, and still lost 41% at the after-hours price.

At NVDA $162.90: stock +4.8% · Nov 20 $155 call +8% · $155 put −94% · $155 straddle −41% · Dec 18 $165 call +14% · Dec 18 $150 put −56%

  • The straddle: cost $14.95 ($1,495) with IV at 135%. If NVDA opens at $162.90 and the Nov IV drops to about 55%, it's worth about $8.79: −$616. At the overnight $156.94 it's about $5.63: −$932. A $7 move was never going to pay for a $15 bet.
  • The call buyer ($155 C at $7.725): about $8.36 at $162.90 (+$64), about $3.80 at $156.94 (−$393). A 4.8% move in your favor earned 8%.
  • The put buyer ($155 P at $7.225): about $0.43 at $162.90 (−$680), about $1.82 at $156.94 (−$541).
  • The December buyer: the Dec 18 $165 call closed $7.70 with IV 65%. With IV around 50% after the report it's about $8.76 at $162.90 (+$106) and $6.06 at $156.94 (−$164). More time means less crush, which is why our plays live in Dec–Jan.
  • The rule we follow because of this: no holding through earnings within a week. Tomorrow we buy after the crush, when IV/realized drops from about 1.45 (EXPENSIVE) to about 1.1 (FAIR).

9. Bull case vs bear case from here

Bull: the numbers were the best in the group's history: a $7B beat, a guide above the Street, a raised fiscal 2028, $43.8B of free cash flow and $227B of buyback firepower. On your chart, the 0.5 has held two 2-day closes after two wicks under it, RSI is 22.5 (deeply stretched), and the after-hours high cleared the last 2-day high. At about 19 times trailing earnings, it's the cheapest it has been in this cycle.

Bear: on your map, the 2.0, 1.618, 1.382 and 0.786 all failed in order since October, and the 2-day highs have fallen eight times in a row. The guide only met the whisper, and four of the last five beats fell the next day. The pop faded from +4.8% to +1.0% before midnight. The CEO seat is empty, the investigation is open, and the balance sheet is now underwriting its customers while the Fed is pricing hikes.

My position: the bear case wins on the trend, the bull case wins the next few days. I think the earnings take away the "is demand cracking" fear, so the $155 area holds near term, but the stock doesn't get its multiple back while the CEO chair is empty. I expect a bounce that stalls at $170. I'm about 60/40 on that. What changes my mind: a 2-day close over $170.22 (your 0.786, the double-bottom neckline and the straddle top) opens $182.67 (the 14-day) and then the $201–204 band, and I'd drop the stall view. A close under $155.33 tells me the market doesn't care about the numbers, and $140.93 is next.

Even the cut targets sit about 27–62% above the overnight price ($156.94); the gap is governance, not earnings.

12. Your INTC puts

You own 2 INTC Nov 20 $50 puts, bought at $0.50 on Nov 16 ($100). They closed $0.62/$0.65 (about $127, +$27), with INTC at $55.17 after a low of $52.42. Tonight INTC rose to $56.67 after hours with the chips and sat at $55.52 overnight.

What would change this read

  • A 2-day close over $170.22 (bull) or under $155.33 (bear) on NVDA.
  • The Dec 9 Fed decision and the Oct FOMC minutes Wednesday at 2 pm: a hiking Fed raises the cost of every lease Nvidia guarantees.
  • A named permanent CEO, or new findings from the investigation. Huang testifies Dec 1. Next report: late February 2027 (date not found).

Confidence and sources

Solid: the results, guide and commitments (company release, CFO commentary, transcript). Thinner: consensus varies by provider ($108.7B–$109.3B revenue; $124.4B–$125.5B for the Q4 guide); after-hours prices move by the minute (ours are Webull at 8 pm and about 11 pm ET); option values for the open are model estimates. Bloomberg and CNBC pages could not be opened, so their points come from outlets quoting them.

What's going on

The forces behind Tuesday

The Fed is pricing hikes, and Tuesday's speakers leaned into it

We see
St. Louis Fed president Musalem: the economy "will likely require several interest rate increases before the spring of 2027." New York's Williams said inflation "is not moving in the right direction." Markets price a 91–97% chance of a 25bp hike on Dec 9 from 3.75–4.00%.
What it means
Higher-for-longer hits long-duration names and anything financed with debt, including the leases Nvidia now guarantees. Financials were the worst sector (−1.9%), V fell 2.3%.
Wrong if
The October FOMC minutes Wednesday at 2 pm show the hike camp is small, or Thursday's data comes in soft.
Touches
V, PLTR, NOW, HOOD, ORCL, TLT

Money left software for the new AI listing

We see
Salesforce −9.5% (its worst day since May 2024), Intuit −7.2%, the software ETF IGV −3.3%, NOW −6.5%, MSFT −2.3%, PLTR −2.4%. Anthropic prices its IPO Wednesday evening ($70–78 range) and trades Thursday as ANT. A SemiAnalysis report also cut its out-year AI chip spending estimates by 19–41%.
What it means
Funds are selling the software they own to make room for the new name. That's a supply problem for software, not a demand problem, and it usually ends when the deal prices.
Wrong if
Software keeps falling after ANT starts trading Thursday. Then it's about AI eating software, not about a deal.
Touches
NOW, PLTR, SHOP, MSFT, ORCL

The data was soft where it matters for the Fed's other mandate

We see
Industrial production fell 0.4% (expected +0.1%). The NAHB builders' index fell to 25 (expected 29), its lowest since April 2012, with 46% of builders cutting prices. Retail sales rose 0.2% (expected 0.1%). Import prices rose 1.1%.
What it means
Growth is slowing while prices are still rising. That's the worst mix for a hiking Fed, and why the 2-year fell only 3bp on weak data.
Wrong if
Housing starts Wednesday 8:30 (about 1.23M expected) beat and the NAHB was a one-off.
Touches
SPY, IWM, HD-type names; BA (industrial production)

The breadth tells you it was broad selling, not one sector

We see
All 11 sectors fell; 75 S&P stocks rose and 426 fell. Equal-weight RSP fell 1.45% against SPY's 1.0%. Goldman says CTAs are now about $3B short after selling $46.5B in a month, and hedge funds' tech long/short ratio is the lowest since 2016.
What it means
Positioning is already very light. That's fuel for a sharp bounce if Nvidia's numbers calm the AI fear. The VIX at 25 with an Extreme Fear reading of 25 says the same.
Wrong if
SPY closes under $725, the double top's target, and the CTAs sell more instead of covering.
Touches
SPY, QQQ, IWM

The defensive sectors didn't defend: utilities and staples fell more than tech. When everything falls together it's positioning and rates, not a story about one industry.

The market in one picture

The double top (Oct 21 $774.44, Nov 4 $775.64) broke its $750.36 neckline on Nov 16. Its measured target is $725.08, and Tuesday's low ($727.00) stopped $1.92 short of it, right at the 200-day ($729.79). When a pattern's target and the 200-day land on the same spot, that's where buyers usually show up. They did, for a day.

Bull case: a held 200-day, RSI 37.5, light positioning and an after-hours bid (+0.7% to $737.61) could lift SPY back to the 61.8% at $740.33. Bear case: price is under the 14 ($750.92), 30 ($761.44) and 50-day ($762.89), and the 14 is falling. I lean bear until SPY closes over $740.33. A close under $725 changes the conversation from "pullback" to "correction."

Fib in action · NVDA 2-day

Wicks test a level; closes decide it

Concept: a level holds on the close, not on the wick. On your 2-day NVDA chart, the 0.5 extension sits at $155.33 (C $129.31 + 0.5 × ($216.66 − $164.61) = $129.31 + $26.02 = $155.33).

Two 2-day candles have now traded through it: Nov 12–13 went to $148.80, and Nov 16–17 to $150.33. Both closed back above it ($162.85, then $155.46, 13 cents over). On your timeframe the level held twice, even though a daily chart would show it broken intraday four times. That's why we judge your levels on the drawing's own close.

What it means for a trade: the call's stop is a close under $155.33, not a touch. The target is the next level up, your 0.786 at $170.22, and the strike that points to is the $170. If a 2-day candle closes under $155.33, the same logic flips: the put's target is the $140.93 down-extension.
